subject: paediatrics
title: Glomerular diseases: nephrotic versus nephritic syndromes

steps.tx: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema. The child shows puffy eyelids, ascites, **hypercholesterolaemia**, and infection or thrombosis risk from urinary protein losses. **Minimal change disease** is the common steroid responsive cause in young children, while focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and membranous disease are considered when hypertension, haematuria, or steroid resistance appears. Urine dipstick, protein creatinine ratio, microscopy, daily weight, and blood pressure prove and track the disease.
steps.say: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy protein loss through the glomerular filter. Albumin falls and fluid leaves vessels into tissues. The face looks puffy and ascites may develop in severe disease. Cholesterol rises because the liver responds to protein loss. Daily weight and urine testing track remission and relapse reliably.

vis.alt: Diagram comparing pediatric nephrotic and nephritic syndromes, highlighting clinical signs, urine findings, and glomerular pathology.
vis.caption: Key differences: Nephrotic (proteinuria, edema) vs. Nephritic (hematuria, hypertension)

steps.tx: Prednisolone induces remission in most children with nephrotic syndrome and the response predicts prognosis. Daily induction is followed by alternate day tapering, while **remission** means protein free urine and relapse means proteinuria returns, often after infection. Frequent relapsers may need cyclophosphamide, steroid resistant disease needs biopsy and calcineurin inhibitors, and difficult courses may need **rituximab** or levamisole. Monitor growth, blood pressure, sugars, cataract, home urine dips, and defer live vaccines during immunosuppression.
steps.say: Steroid treatment can induce remission in most children with this disease. Remission is defined when the urine becomes free of protein again. Relapse often follows an infection and parents detect it with home dipsticks. Frequent relapses need steroid sparing treatment after specialist review. Growth and blood pressure need monitoring because prolonged steroids cause harm.

steps.tx: Nephritic syndrome presents with haematuria, hypertension, and oliguria from glomerular inflammation. **Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis** follows sore throat or skin infection with raised ASO and low C3, while **IgA nephropathy** flares with concurrent respiratory infection. Henoch Schonlein purpura, lupus, and membranoproliferative disease are other causes, and rapidly progressive disease with crescents needs urgent biopsy. Salt and fluid restriction and antihypertensives control pressure, and C3 normalisation is followed in post streptococcal disease.
steps.say: Nephritic syndrome inflames the glomerulus and reduces urine output. The urine looks cola coloured and blood pressure rises quickly. Post streptococcal disease follows throat or skin infection. Complement falls in many immune mediated causes. Salt restriction and pressure control protect the child while recovery is monitored.

steps.tx: This glomerular image shows dark **subepithelial humps** on the basement membrane with effaced podocyte foot processes and infiltrating neutrophils below fenestrated endothelium. Complement activation and low serum C3 explain the inflammatory nephritic picture after streptococcal infection. For exams, humps point toward **post streptococcal glomerulonephritis**, and the combination of cola coloured urine, hypertension, and low C3 should not be confused with steroid responsive minimal change disease.
steps.say: This image shows immune deposits sitting above the glomerular basement membrane. Neutrophils gather inside the capillary and complement becomes activated. The picture explains haematuria and reduced filtration in nephritic disease. Cola coloured urine with hypertension and low complement should point toward post streptococcal disease in an exam stem.

steps.tx: Supportive care protects the kidney and the child during glomerular disease. Judicious salt and protein intake, **diuretics** for oedema, albumin infusion for hypovolaemia, and **ACE inhibitors** for persistent proteinuria all help, while statins and anticoagulation suit selected persistent cases. Cushingoid appearance affects body image and needs psychological support, and transition to adult nephrology must be planned. Missed hypertension crisis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and acute kidney injury are dangerous traps that need early recognition.
steps.say: Supportive care controls oedema and protects long term kidney function. Diuretics remove excess fluid when circulation remains adequate. Drugs that block angiotensin reduce persistent proteinuria. Blood pressure needs regular checks because crises develop silently. The family also needs support because steroid effects change appearance and confidence.
